demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
David has been a forester for thirty years, and for most of that time, the woods were the only place he felt truly competent. That all changed eight months ago, on a crisp autumn afternoon. He was operating the skidder, pulling felled logs up a steep grade, a task he'd performed thousands of times. Leo, a seasonal worker not much older than his own son, was spotting for him. The ground was softer than it looked after an overnight rain. David felt the machine lurch, a sudden, sickening slide to the left. In the split second it took him to correct, the log stack shifted. He remembers the crack of splintering pine and Leo's shout, cut short. The weight of his experience, his mastery of the machine and the terrain, had vanished in an instant, replaced by the image of Leo pinned beneath the load.

In the months that followed, the forest became a hostile territory. His supervisor, trying to be helpful, assigned him to inventory duties on the flatter, safer plots. But even the physical proximity to the familiar woods was enough to bring on a cold sweat. He found he couldn't work. The company eventually moved him to a desk, a gesture of kindness that felt like a confirmation of his failure. He was no longer the man who could read a landscape at a glance; he was the man who couldn't be trusted with machinery. He had come to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him. This conviction settled deep in his bones, a certainty that there was something intrinsically wrong with him, a fundamental flaw that had made the accident inevitable.

The memories are not just images; they are physical events. He can be standing in his own kitchen when, without warning, his body reenacts the moment. His hands will clench as if gripping the joysticks, the muscles in his back and shoulders seizing in the exact posture of bracing for the skidder's lurch. The sensation is often followed by a flash of white-hot rage directed entirely at himself-for his carelessness, for his arrogance in thinking he had the situation under control. Then comes the grief, a hollow, crushing weight for the life he altered. He thinks of Leo, who now walks with a permanent limp and can no longer do the work he loved. Seeing any young man with a similar build or a familiar gait can stop David in his tracks, his breath catching in his throat.

The sense of a fundamentally unsafe world has bled out from the forest into his daily life. The split-second unpredictability of the accident has convinced him that danger can erupt from anywhere, at any time. In a crowded grocery store, he finds himself watching other people with a hawk-like intensity, scanning for any sign of a threat. He watches their hands, their eyes, interpreting a sudden movement or an intense gaze as a precursor to harm. He is certain that others can see his weakness, his failure, and might try to take advantage of it. If a stranger approaches him too quickly down an aisle, even just to reach for a can of soup, his body tenses and he feels an urgent need to retreat, his heart pounding with a primal fear. He gives everyone a wide berth, his mind constantly calculating escape routes. His wife, Sarah, notices he can never relax, even on their own porch. He's always scanning the street, braced for a threat he can't name but is certain is coming. Any sharp, unexpected pain in his own body-a twinge in his back when he lifts a bag of dog food-can still catapult him back to the splintering sound of the logs, a visceral reminder of how quickly safety can be annihilated.

David finally sought help after a visit from Leo a few weeks ago. The young man came to the house, leaning on his cane, and spoke with a forgiveness David felt he had no right to receive. After he left, David sat in his truck for an hour, overwhelmed by a grief so total it felt like annihilation. He realized he was not just living with a memory, but being erased by it. He is here now because the man he used to be is gone, and he is terrified that the broken, vulnerable person who remains is all he will ever be again.

missing.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
missing.explanation: The vignette describes the patient's fear of harming strangers, not a fear of being harmed by them. The patient is described as watching others closely and keeping his distance because he is 'terrified he will somehow harm them', which is the opposite of the reported symptom.

missing.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
missing.explanation: The vignette states that the patient watches others 'not because he fears they will harm him, but because he is terrified he will somehow harm them.' This directly contradicts the self-reported symptom's focus on perceiving threats from others.
